prompt.context: Your client is a manufacturer of food processing and preparation equipment sold to households and restaurants. 70% of goods are imported from China and Italy; 30% are manufactured locally. The client has been in the industry for over 80 years and has a very strong brand name. The client has experienced a 1% decline in sales for each of the last 5 years and a comparable drop in earnings over the same period.
prompt.question: The client would like to understand why sales and earnings have dropped and how to address the issues.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the market and how fast is it growing?
clarifying_info.a: This is a mature market with low growth. The client services the entire U.S., split equally among Northeast, Northwest, and South.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the client's customers and what is the revenue split?
clarifying_info.a: 95% of revenue comes from restaurants; the remaining 5% comes to households. Products are sold through buying groups that represent collections of restaurants.
New competitors have entered the market and copied the client's products. Competitors have also begun offering complete kitchen solutions that include items the client does not currently produce.

COGS: a slight increase in the price of imported goods, about 2% every 3 years. Production costs have not changed. Distribution costs have increased slightly due to higher fuel costs from shipping; the client contracts with UPS or FedEx.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client's pricing compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The client has the best brand in the industry in terms of quality and recognition and prices at a slight premium. Locally manufactured goods have slightly higher margins.
The mix of products has changed slightly in the past few years.

framework: Diagnose revenue decline: volume vs. price; which product lines / customer segments are driving the drop
Diagnose cost pressures: COGS (imported goods price increase), distribution (fuel costs), production
Competitive dynamics: new entrants copying products, competitors offering complete kitchen solutions
Product line analysis: household vs. restaurant segment profitability; assess whether to grow, maintain, or divest household business
Revenue improvement levers: pricing, promotion, channel strategy, bundling, new revenue streams
Cost improvement levers: shift to local production, renegotiate with foreign suppliers

questions.prompt: What is driving the revenue decline and what levers can the client pull to reverse it?
questions.guidance: Strong answers explore volume vs. price, identify that competitors are undercutting on price and offering complete solutions the client lacks, and propose: (1) raising price premium to reinforce brand; (2) marketing on chef reality shows, trade shows, and high-end chains; (3) selling direct to restaurants to bypass buying groups; (4) bundling companion products; (5) launching a 'certified pre-owned' line given high restaurant turnover.

questions.prompt: Should the client invest in or divest its household business (5% of revenue)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask: Is the household market growing faster than the restaurant market? Is the household segment more or less profitable than the restaurant segment? If household is growing and more profitable, explore how to grow it (expanded distribution, targeted marketing, new SKUs for home cooks). If household is smaller/less profitable, consider divesting or spinning it off to focus on the core restaurant business.

questions.prompt: What cost levers are available to improve margins?
questions.guidance: Imported goods (70% of goods) have a 2% price increase every 3 years and lower margins than locally produced goods. Strong answers explore: (1) building or renting additional local production capacity to reduce reliance on imports; (2) squeezing foreign suppliers to reduce import costs; (3) reviewing distribution contracts with UPS/FedEx given rising fuel costs.

questions.prompt: The client is considering entering a 'certified pre-owned' (CPO) equipment business. What are the benefits and risks?
questions.guidance: Benefit: high-margin revenue stream capitalizing on the high restaurant failure rate; strong brand lends credibility to certified refurbished goods. Risk: cannibalization of new equipment sales to restaurants considering buying used instead of new.

brainstorming.prompt: What would you want to know about the household (consumer) segment before making a recommendation on it?

categories.name: Market attractiveness
ideas: Is the household market growing faster than the restaurant market?
What is the total addressable market size for household kitchen equipment?
Are consumer preferences shifting toward premium home cooking equipment?

categories.name: Profitability
ideas: What are the margins on household products vs. restaurant products?
What are the distinct cost structures (packaging, distribution, returns) for household vs. restaurant channels?
How does price sensitivity differ between household consumers and restaurant buyers?

categories.name: Competitive position
ideas: Is the client's brand equally strong with consumers as it is with restaurants?
Are competitors also targeting household customers?
Are there e-commerce or DTC channels competitors are using that the client is not?

categories.name: Strategic fit
ideas: Does household require different SKUs and R&D investment than the restaurant line?
Would growing household distract from the core restaurant business?
Could household serve as a brand-building halo for the restaurant segment?

recommendation: Raise prices modestly to reinforce the premium brand image and capture more of restaurants' willingness to pay
Invest in promotions targeting high-end restaurant chains and chef media (reality shows, trade shows) to defend and grow market share
Evaluate direct sales to restaurant groups to bypass buying groups and capture more margin
Explore product bundling to increase average order value and stickiness
Shift more production to local facilities over time to improve margins; renegotiate contracts with foreign suppliers in the near term
Conduct a focused profitability analysis of the household segment; if unprofitable or subscale, divest to sharpen focus on the core restaurant business
risks: Entering the certified pre-owned market could cannibalize new equipment sales
Competitors may match any promotions or bundling strategies, eroding the advantage
Customers may resist a higher price premium, accelerating share loss to lower-cost competitors
Localizing production could strain quality control and require significant capital investment
next_steps: Commission a detailed P&L by product line and customer segment to confirm where margin erosion is greatest
Conduct customer research with buying groups and restaurant operators to gauge price sensitivity and product gaps
Build a business case for incremental local production capacity with break-even analysis
Pilot a bundling or CPO program with a select set of restaurant customers before broad rollout
